status: drafted via multi-agent workflow grounded in the real extracted verse text, adversarially fact-checked and corrected
notes:
Full direct read of the extracted Ethiopian-translation text (Assets/Resources/Verses/Ethiopian/joshua_6.json, 24 chapters, 658 verses) confirms this book is textually and structurally identical to the standard KJV-tradition Joshua narrative -- same 24 chapters, same event order, same wording throughout (spies/Rahab, Jordan crossing, circumcision at Gilgal, Jericho's fall, Achan's sin, Ai, Gibeonite deception, the five-king coalition and the long day at Gibeon, the northern coalition at the waters of Merom, the land allotment (Caleb at Hebron, Zelophehad's five daughters, the seven-tribe lot at Shiloh), the cities of refuge, the Levitical cities, the eastern-tribes' altar-of-witness dispute, and Joshua's farewell speech, covenant renewal at Shechem, and death/burial at Timnathserah). This is a genuine finding from reading the real text, not an assumption -- it stands in real contrast to this same Ethiopian Bible's confirmed structural divergence elsewhere (its own 9-chapter Ezra, matching the 1 Esdras tradition rather than the 10-chapter Masoretic Ezra). No unique Ethiopian-canon content, extra chapters, or reordering was found anywhere in this book.

All ids are suffixed _ethiopian to avoid collision with the existing plain-named KJV CharacterIndex ids for the same figures. Naming collisions carried forward from the same real-text patterns already documented for this book in the KJV index, re-verified against this translation's own wording: Jabin king of Hazor (Josh 11) shares a name only, not a stated identity, with a later Jabin king of Hazor in Judges; Phinehas son of Eleazar (Josh 22) is distinct from the later Phinehas son of Eli; Debir is used both as a king's personal name (Josh 10:3) and, within this very book, as a Canaanite city name (Josh 10:38-39, 15:15); Japhia king of Lachish (Josh 10) shares a name only with a much later son of David; among Zelophehad's five daughters, Noah shares a name only with the flood patriarch, Milcah shares a name only with Nahor's wife in Genesis, and Tirzah shares a name only with the Canaanite city later listed among the defeated kings (Josh 12:24) and later still a northern-kingdom capital -- none of these are asserted as the same person/place. Zelophehad's five daughters (Josh 17:3) act and speak as one undifferentiated group in the text, so per this index's collective-group convention only Mahlah (named first, both here and in Numbers 26:33) receives a full manager entry, with her four sisters as loyalty-boost submanagers. The five kings of Josh 10:3,5 are handled the same way: Adonizedek as the coalition's initiating major, the other four as cost-cutter submanagers, since the text differentiates none of their individual actions beyond being named and executed together. Geographic-only material (the ~25 undifferentiated kings of ch12 beyond the five of ch10 and Jabin of ch11, the extensive tribal boundary/town-name lists of ch13, 15-19, 21, and the unnamed spies/twelve stone-bearers/ten princes) is captured in genealogyLists rather than invented as individual characters, matching the same judgment call already validated for this book's KJV index.

characters.name: Joshua

genealogy.note: Josh 1:1 (this translation): 'the LORD spake unto Joshua the son of Nun, Moses' minister.' No further family named within this book's own text.

verses.note: Commissioned by the LORD after Moses' death; charged to 'be strong and of a good courage.'
Leads Israel across the Jordan on dry ground behind the priest-borne ark.
Meets 'the captain of the LORD's host' near Jericho and is told to loose his shoe, 'for the place whereon thou standest is holy.'
Leads the seven-day march and trumpet-blowing around Jericho until its wall falls.
Commands the sun to stand still over Gibeon and the moon over the valley of Ajalon.
Farewell charge to Israel's elders and officers in his old age.
Renews the covenant at Shechem: 'as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.'
Dies at 110 and is buried in Timnathserah in mount Ephraim.

ageEvents.event: Death, called 'the servant of the LORD'

funFacts: At his death he is given the title 'the servant of the LORD' (Josh 24:29), a title this same book reserves for Moses at its opening (Josh 1:1).

characters.name: Rahab

genealogy.note: Her father's household (unnamed individually) is spared with her, Josh 6:23,25. This book's own text says nothing of a later marriage or descendants; no such claim is made here.

verses.note: Hides the two unnamed spies Joshua sends to Jericho, misdirects the king's pursuers, and lets them down by a cord through her window; agrees to hang a scarlet line as a sign.
Spared with her household when Jericho is destroyed; 'she dwelleth in Israel even unto this day.'

funFacts: Explicitly called 'Rahab the harlot' in this translation's own text (Josh 2:1; 6:17,25).

genealogy.note: Full stated line: 'Achan, the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah' (Josh 7:1,18). His sons and daughters die with him (Josh 7:24) but are never named individually, so no separate entries are given for them.

verses.note: Introduced as having 'committed a trespass in the accursed thing' from Jericho's spoil.
Identified by lot; confesses to taking a Babylonish garment, silver, and a wedge of gold; stoned and burned in the valley of Achor.
Retrospectively invoked as a warning by the western tribes: 'that man perished not alone in his iniquity.'

characters.name: The Gibeonites

genealogy.note: Represented collectively -- no individual Gibeonite is named in Josh 9-10. Treated as one narrative unit per this index's convention for an undifferentiated named group.

verses.note: Disguise themselves as travelers from a distant land with worn sacks, mouldy bread, and patched clothes to trick Israel into a covenant; once discovered, made 'hewers of wood and drawers of water' rather than destroyed, since Israel had sworn by the LORD.
Besieged by the five-king coalition for making peace with Israel, prompting Joshua's rescue march and the long day at Gibeon.

funFacts: Their trick worked specifically because Israel 'asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD' (Josh 9:14).

characters.name: Adonizedek

genealogy.note: No family named. King of Jerusalem.

verses.note: Organizes a five-king Amorite coalition (naming Hoham, Piram, Japhia, and Debir individually) to besiege Gibeon for making peace with Israel.
Hides with the other four kings in the cave at Makkedah; captured, executed, and hanged on trees until evening.

funFacts: His name ('lord of righteousness') invites comparison to 'Melchizedek' ('king of righteousness'), an earlier king of the same city in Genesis 14:18 -- a name-pattern similarity only; this book's text nowhere states a family or identity link between them.

genealogy.note: No family named.

verses.note: Named king of Hebron, summoned by Adonizedek.
Brought out of the cave at Makkedah and executed with the other four kings.

genealogy.note: No family named.

verses.note: Named king of Jarmuth, summoned by Adonizedek.
Brought out of the cave at Makkedah and executed with the other four kings.

genealogy.note: No family named here. NAMING COLLISION: shares his name only with one of David's sons born at Jerusalem, named far later in scripture -- a different, unrelated person.

verses.note: Named king of Lachish, summoned by Adonizedek.
Brought out of the cave at Makkedah and executed with the other four kings.

genealogy.note: No family named. NAMING COLLISION within this very book: 'Debir' is used here as a personal name (king of Eglon), but 'Debir' is also a Canaanite city in Judah's hill country, formerly called Kirjathsepher, later taken by Othniel (Josh 10:38-39; 15:15-17) -- same word, two distinct referents.

verses.note: Named king of Eglon, summoned by Adonizedek.
Brought out of the cave at Makkedah and executed with the other four kings.

characters.name: Jabin

genealogy.note: No family named. NAMING COLLISION: a different Jabin king of Hazor appears generations later in Judges as the oppressor defeated via Deborah, Barak, and Jael -- this index treats the two as separate figures who merely share a name and city-title, not the same person.

verses.note: Assembles a northern coalition of kings at the waters of Merom; defeated by Joshua, and Hazor, 'the head of all those kingdoms,' is burned.

funFacts: Hazor is the only city among the defeated northern coalition that Israel burns (Josh 11:13).

characters.name: Caleb

genealogy.note: Called 'the son of Jephunneh the Kenezite' (Josh 14:6,14). His brother Othniel is called 'the son of Kenaz' (Josh 15:17); whether Caleb's own 'Kenezite' label reflects the same Kenaz as a shared father or a broader clan name is not made explicit by this book's text and is left unresolved here rather than silently decided.

verses.note: Claims Hebron at Gilgal, citing Moses' oath after the spy mission from Kadeshbarnea forty-five years earlier.
Given Hebron; offers his daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever takes Kirjathsepher (Debir).

ageEvents.event: Sent by Moses from Kadeshbarnea to spy out the land
Claims his inheritance at Hebron, forty-five years after the spying mission

funFacts: Explicitly called 'the Kenezite' (Josh 14:6,14) yet receives a full inheritance within Judah's territory.

genealogy.note: No further genealogy given beyond her marriage to Othniel.

verses.note: Married to Othniel after he takes Kirjathsepher; asks Caleb for 'the upper springs and the nether springs' -- the source of this tier's name.

genealogy.note: Called 'the son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb' (Josh 15:17) -- this book's own wording is ambiguous whether 'the brother of Caleb' modifies Othniel or Kenaz; hedged, not resolved, per this index's rule against silently deciding textual cruxes.

verses.note: Takes Kirjathsepher and receives Achsah as wife.

genealogy.note: Full stated line for her father: 'Zelophehad, the son of Hepher, the son of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh' (Josh 17:3). Named first among her sisters. The five daughters act and speak as an undifferentiated group in this book's text, so only Mahlah is given a full manager entry, with her sisters as submanagers.

verses.note: Comes with her sisters before Eleazar, Joshua, and the princes, citing the LORD's earlier command to Moses; receives an inheritance among their father's brethren.

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION: this 'Noah' (a daughter of Zelophehad) shares her name only with the flood patriarch Noah -- two unrelated figures who share an English spelling.

verses.note: Named among Zelophehad's five daughters.

genealogy.note: A town called Bethhoglah ('house of Hoglah') sits on the Judah/Benjamin border within this same book (Josh 15:6; 18:19,21); the text never links the town's name to this daughter, so this is flagged only as a shared root, not a claimed identification.

verses.note: Named among Zelophehad's five daughters.

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION: shares her name only with Milcah, wife of Nahor (Abraham's brother), named repeatedly in Genesis -- a different, much earlier figure.

verses.note: Named among Zelophehad's five daughters.

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION within this very book: shares her name only with the Canaanite city of Tirzah, whose king is listed among the 31 defeated by Joshua (Josh 12:24) -- same word, two distinct referents.

verses.note: Named among Zelophehad's five daughters.

characters.name: Cities of Refuge
characters.purpose: Establishes six cities (three west, three east of the Jordan) where a person who kills another 'unawares and unwittingly' (Josh 20:3) may flee from the avenger of blood and receive a hearing before the congregation, remaining safe until the death of the serving high priest -- teaching that unintentional killing is judged differently from murder, and that justice requires due process rather than immediate vengeance.

verses.note: Purpose and procedure of the cities of refuge, relaying what the LORD had earlier commanded through Moses.
Names the six cities: Kedesh, Shechem, and Kirjatharba (Hebron) west of Jordan; Bezer, Ramoth in Gilead, and Golan in Bashan east of Jordan.

funFacts: This translation's own phrase is 'unawares and unwittingly' (Josh 20:3).

characters.name: Levitical Cities
characters.purpose: Assigns the Levites forty-eight cities with surrounding pasture lands out of the other tribes' inheritances, since the Levites received no territorial inheritance of their own -- teaching that the priestly/Levitical calling is itself their portion, with the LORD as their inheritance, while still providing practically for their material needs through the rest of the nation.

verses.note: The Levites' request, made per the LORD's command through Moses, brought to Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal heads at Shiloh.
Summary: forty-eight cities with their suburbs given to the Levites.

genealogy.note: Josh 22:13,32: 'Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest.' NAMING COLLISION: a different Phinehas, son of Eli, appears far later in 1 Samuel -- an explicitly separate priestly line, not descended from this Phinehas or from Eleazar.

verses.note: Sent with ten tribal princes to confront Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh over the altar they built by the Jordan.
Satisfied by their explanation that the altar was meant as a witness, not for sacrifice; reports back and war is averted.

genealogy.note: His descent from Aaron is common scriptural knowledge rather than something restated within this book's own text, so it is noted here, not asserted as a claim this book itself makes. NAMING COLLISION: distinct from other Eleazars named elsewhere in scripture, e.g. Eleazar son of Abinadab or Eleazar the Ahohite among David's mighty men.

verses.note: Co-presides with Joshua and the tribal heads over the distribution of Canaan's inheritance by lot.
Receives Zelophehad's daughters' inheritance claim alongside Joshua.
Receives the Levites' request for cities.
Dies; buried in a hill belonging to Phinehas his son in mount Ephraim.

genealogyLists.note: Bulk/unresolved references, kept out of the character list above -- almost entirely geographic (place names, boundary markers, town lists) with no individual personal action attached, per the same judgment call already validated for this book's KJV index.
genealogyLists.thirty_one_kings_ch12: Josh 12 lists 31 kings defeated west of the Jordan under Joshua (12:7-24), plus Sihon and Og defeated earlier under Moses east of Jordan (12:1-6). Beyond the five kings of the ch10 coalition and Jabin of Hazor (ch11) -- all given full entries above -- the remaining roughly 25 kings are identified only by the city they ruled, with no individual action differentiated in the text.
genealogyLists.sihon_and_og_ch12: Josh 12:1-6 recaps Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, kings defeated earlier under Moses -- their narrative belongs to the book of Numbers, referenced here only in summary.
genealogyLists.tribal_boundary_and_town_lists_ch13_15_1: Chapters 13, 15-19, and 21 give detailed tribal territory boundaries, town-name lists, and Levitical-city lists -- almost entirely geographic, beyond Caleb (ch14-15) and Zelophehad's daughters (ch17:3-6), both already given full entries above.
genealogyLists.ten_princes_ch22: Josh 22:13-14 sends Phinehas 'and with him ten princes, of each chief house a prince throughout all the tribes' to confront the eastern tribes over the altar of witness; none of the ten is individually named.
genealogyLists.reuben_gad_manasseh_respondents_ch22: The Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh who built the altar of witness (Josh 22:10-34) respond and are quoted collectively; no individual leader on their side is named within this chapter.
genealogyLists.unnamed_spies_ch2: The 'two men to spy secretly' whom Joshua sends to Jericho, and whom Rahab hides (Josh 2:1), are never named.
genealogyLists.twelve_men_ch3_4: The twelve men chosen 'out of every tribe a man' to carry stones from the dry Jordan bed (Josh 3:12; 4:2-8) are not individually named.
